extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants and IP practitioners (patent attorneys/prosecutors)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the legal standards for satisfying the 35 U.S.C. § 112 written description requirement for patent claims (especially genus and functional claims), based on the Ariad v. Eli Lilly en banc Federal Circuit decision. Emphasizes disclosure sufficiency, illustrative examples, and particular issues in the biological arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate written description requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit confirmed that 35 U.S.C. § 112 contains a written description requirement that is separate from the enablement requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The en banc court stated that "a separate requirement to describe one's invention is basic to patent law," and reaffirmed existing precedent that written description is a standalone statutory obligation. This is not merely an enablement inquiry; applicants must separately satisfy written description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description applies beyond priority/new-matter contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: The written description requirement extends beyond priority questions (new matter/parent application support) and must be satisfied by originally-filed claims as well as amended claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court stated the requirement "extends beyond a priority context, such as in questions of new matter or whether claims are supported by a parent application, and is a requirement that even originally-filed claims must satisfy."

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus claims require disclosure of representative species or common structural features
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that cover multiple embodiments or species (genus claims) can lack written description if the specification does not disclose representative species or structural features common to the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting prior case law, the court held "a sufficient description of a genus instead requires the disclosure of either a representative number of species falling within the scope of the genus or structural features common to the members of the genus so that one of skill in the art can 'visualize or recognize' the members of the genus." Without such disclosure, genus claims may be unsupported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional claims require species support (cannot merely claim results)
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional claims that simply claim a desired result without describing species that achieve that result are defective unless the applicant shows possession of species sufficient to support the claimed functional genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court held an adequate description "must demonstrate that the applicant has made a generic invention that achieves the claimed result and do so by showing that the applicant has invented species sufficient to support a claim to the functionally-defined genus." Functional claiming is especially scrutinized in the biological arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise definition of species — structure, formula, name, properties, etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Adequate written description typically requires precise definitions of species (by structure, formula, chemical name, physical properties, or other properties) sufficient to distinguish the genus from other materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court explained that adequate written description requires a precise definition (e.g., structure, formula, chemical name, physical properties) of species within the genus so the genus is distinguished from other materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation between structure and function can satisfy written description
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional claim language can satisfy the written description requirement when the art has established a correlation between structure and function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court cited Enzo Biochem, Inc. v. Gen-Probe Inc. to note that where a correlation between structure and function is established in the art, functional language may meet the written description requirement. In such cases, disclosing structural features that are known to cause a function can support functional claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad/outer-limits functional claiming is inadequate; obviousness is not enough
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely 'drawing a fence around the outer limits of a purported genus' or providing a description that only renders the invention obvious does not satisfy the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court declared that "merely drawing a fence around the outer limits of a purported genus is not an adequate substitute for describing a variety of materials constituting the genus," and that "a description that merely renders the invention obvious does not satisfy the requirement." Applicants must describe a sufficient variety or defining features, not just broad boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Possession in the disclosure" standard; reduction to practice insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must show 'possession in the disclosure'; actual possession outside the specification (e.g., later reduction to practice) is not sufficient. Conversely, reduction to practice is neither necessary nor sufficient to satisfy written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court admitted "possession of the invention" was vague and preferred the phrase "possession in the disclosure." It held that "an 'actual possession' or reduction to practice outside the specification is not enough to satisfy the written description requirement," and that reduction to practice is neither necessary nor sufficient. However, the existence of working examples in the specification, or prophetic examples, can suffice to establish written description support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional claims must recite sufficient materials to accomplish the function (esp. in biological arts)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patent claims a genus by function or result, the specification must recite sufficient materials to accomplish that function; claims that merely recite the problem and claim all solutions are invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court warned that functional claims will fail when they "merely recite a description of the problem to be solved while claiming all solutions to it and … cover any compound later actually invented and determined to fall within the claim's functional boundaries — leaving it to the pharmaceutical industry to complete an unfinished invention." This is particularly acute in the biological arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosing unclaimed/planned research without adequate description risks placing subject matter in the public domain
rubrics_metrics.description: Material described in a patent application but not claimed — especially speculative or planned-research disclosures — may be placed in the public domain if not supported by adequate written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cautions applicants not to disclose planned research ideas insufficiently described to support claims, because such subject matter becomes public domain (citing Unique Concepts, Inc. v. Brown). This serves as a procedural warning when drafting disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for concrete examples and a descriptive link between disclosed species and claimed function (case-specific biotech lessons)
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification must provide concrete examples or a descriptive link showing how disclosed molecules/structures achieve the claimed functional activity; mere suggestion or speculative teaching is inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Ariad case facts illustrate this: the court found Ariad's specification lacked sufficient working examples showing inhibition of NF-κB or a descriptive link between disclosed molecules (e.g., tables of sequences) and claimed functional activity. The court discounted post-priority evidence and expert testimony about existence of molecules absent disclosure, and treated speculative plans (e.g., dominantly interfering molecules where key assumptions were unknown) as insufficient.
